core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Constrictive Pericarditis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes explaining to the patient that the rigid calcified pericardium acts like an iron shell preventing the ventricles from filling normally during diastole, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: swollen belly, puffy ankles, and feeling full quickly over 6 months

Key HPI features: 6-month history of progressive abdominal distension, severe leg swelling, and early satiety after eating small meals. Feels chronically exhausted and breathless when walking 100 metres. Treated for pulmonary and pericardial tuberculosis 20 years ago in his home country with a full 9-month course of anti-TB drugs. Recently seen by a gastroenterologist who found normal liver function tests and negative liver serology despite massive ascites.

Objective/Exam findings: Physical exam: marked JVP elevation (+6 cm H2O) demonstrating Kussmaul's sign (paradoxical RISE in JVP during inspiration rather than normal fall, indicating impaired right ventricular filling) and prominent y-descent (Friedreich's sign). Auscultation: early diastolic 'pericardial knock' sound heard at the left sternal border. Abdominal exam: tense ascites and pulsatile, tender hepatomegaly. Chest X-ray or CT chest: shows dense calcification of the pericardial ring. Echocardiogram and Cardiac MRI: thickened, rigid, calcified pericardium (>4mm) with abnormal septal bounce and respiratory variation in ventricular filling (interventricular dependence).
Relevant background/PMH: pericardial/pulmonary tuberculosis 20 years ago, hypertension
Current medications: furosemide 40mg OD with poor reduction of abdominal fluid
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Constrictive Pericarditis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Liver cirrhosis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapidly increasing abdominal swelling with breathlessness.
management_principles: Explain to patient that the rigid calcified pericardium acts like an iron shell preventing the ventricles from filling normally during diastole

Medical optimization: cautious loop diuretic use (furosemide) and aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) to manage peripheral congestion and ascites without excessive preload reduction that could compromise stroke volume
Urgent cardiothoracic surgery referral for definitive surgical pericardiectomy (pericardial stripping)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2025 Concise Clinical Guidance: An ACC Expert Consensus Statement on the Diagnosis and Management of Pericarditis

reference_soap.subjective: 60M with history of pericardial tuberculosis presents with chronic right-sided heart failure symptoms: ascites, peripheral oedema, and fatigue refractory to diuretics, with normal liver serology.
reference_soap.objective: Physical exam: marked JVP elevation (+6 cm H2O) demonstrating Kussmaul's sign (paradoxical RISE in JVP during inspiration rather than normal fall, indicating impaired right ventricular filling) and prominent y-descent (Friedreich's sign). Auscultation: early diastolic 'pericardial knock' sound heard at the left sternal border. Abdominal exam: tense ascites and pulsatile, tender hepatomegaly. Chest X-ray or CT chest: shows dense calcification of the pericardial ring. Echocardiogram and Cardiac MRI: thickened, rigid, calcified pericardium (>4mm) with abnormal septal bounce and respiratory variation in ventricular filling (interventricular dependence).
reference_soap.assessment: Constrictive Pericarditis secondary to remote tuberculous pericarditis. DDx: restrictive cardiomyopathy (cardiac amyloidosis - differentiated by absent pericardial calcification/knock and presence of severe atrial enlargement), cirrhotic liver disease with ascites, right ventricular infarction.
reference_soap.plan: Explain to patient that the rigid calcified pericardium acts like an iron shell preventing the ventricles from filling normally during diastole. Medical optimization: cautious loop diuretic use (furosemide) and aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone) to manage peripheral congestion and ascites without excessive preload reduction that could compromise stroke volume. Urgent cardiothoracic surgery referral for definitive surgical pericardiectomy (pericardial stripping).

learning_objectives: Differentiate constrictive pericarditis from liver cirrhosis when patients present with isolated right heart failure and massive ascites
Identify classical physical findings of constrictive pericarditis: Kussmaul's sign, prominent y-descent, and early diastolic pericardial knock
Correlate remote tuberculous pericardial infection with delayed rigid pericardial calcification decades later
Explain the definitive curative role of surgical pericardiectomy when conservative diuretic management fails

teaching.one_liner: A scarred, rigid pericardium stops the heart filling. Right-sided congestion dominates: swollen belly, swollen ankles, early fullness after eating.
red_flags: Rapidly increasing abdominal swelling with breathlessness

must_ask.say: Does your belly feel full quickly when you eat?
How far up your legs does the swelling go?
Have you ever had tuberculosis, or radiotherapy to your chest?
Have you had heart surgery or been told you had pericarditis before?
Are you breathless walking, or also when you sit still?
Over what period has this built up?

history.answer: My belly has become swollen like a balloon and my ankles are very puffy, and it's been getting worse over the past six months.
The swelling is in my belly and both of my ankles and lower legs. My face and eyelids haven't looked puffy at all.
It started slowly about six months ago, but my abdomen and legs have become much tighter and larger week by week.
My ankles and legs are much puffier by the evening after I have been walking, while my belly stays bloated all day and night.
Yes, whenever I press on my shins with my fingers it leaves deep dents, and my socks leave tight marks on my ankles.
I have gained about six kilograms over the last few months, even though I have actually been eating much less.
No, both legs look equal, and neither leg has any redness, warmth, or sudden cramp-like pain.
I get quite short of breath and worn out after walking just a hundred meters, but I can sleep flat without needing extra pillows.
My urine is normal yellow without bubbles or dark tea color, but the daily amount feels somewhat less than usual.
No, my eyes and skin have not turned yellow, and I have not had any nosebleeds, easy bruising, or black stools.
I get completely full after just a few bites of food because my stomach feels so tight and crowded.
I feel exhausted all the time, but I have not had chills, cold sensitivity, dry skin, or trouble with constipation.
No, I have not had any sore throat, fever, skin boils, or colds in recent months.
No, I haven't taken any long flights, haven't been stuck in bed, and I have never had cancer or taken hormone pills.
I avoid salty foods as much as I can, but being upright on my feet during the day definitely makes my ankles swell more.
A stomach specialist checked me recently and found a large amount of fluid in my belly, but all my liver blood tests and hepatitis checks were completely normal.
Twenty years ago back in my home country, I had tuberculosis affecting both my lungs and the sac around my heart, and I took medication for nine months.
I had that severe inflammation around my heart from tuberculosis twenty years ago, but I have never had heart surgery or radiation to my chest.
I wonder if that old tuberculosis left hard, scarred tissue around my heart that is keeping it from expanding and filling properly.
I am really worried someone will wrongly diagnose me with liver cirrhosis, especially when my liver blood tests were completely fine.
I am hoping you can order a heart scan to see if the lining around my heart has turned into a hard, rigid shell.
Aside from having tuberculosis twenty years ago, I have been treated for high blood pressure for the past eight years.
I stayed in the hospital twenty years ago when they treated my tuberculosis, but I have never had any surgeries.
I take furosemide forty milligrams once daily for water retention, but it barely shrinks my belly, along with my blood pressure pill.
I do not have any allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I do not drink any alcohol at all, and I never have.
I worked as an auto mechanic before retiring, and I immigrated here fifteen years ago. I live with my wife in an apartment.
My father had high blood pressure and passed away in his late seventies, but no one in my family had heart failure or kidney disease.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, pulse 82 beats per minute regular, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius.
Markedly elevated jugular venous pressure at 6 cm above the sternal angle with prominent y-descent and paradoxical rise on inspiration (Kussmaul's sign).
Normal first and second heart sounds with a high-pitched early diastolic sound (pericardial knock) audible along the left sternal border; no murmurs.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields without crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi.
Markedly distended abdomen with shifting dullness and a demonstrable fluid wave, consistent with tense ascites.
Enlarged, pulsatile liver palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin with marked tenderness; spleen is not palpable.
Bilateral symmetrical 3+ pitting edema extending from the feet up to the mid-shins.
Symmetrical calf circumferences with no local tenderness, erythema, warmth, or palpable cord bilaterally.
Anicteric sclerae and pink conjunctivae without pallor or jaundice.
No spider angiomas, palmar erythema, caput medusae, or jaundice.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, non-tender, and without palpable nodules or bruits.
No periorbital edema or facial puffiness; extraocular movements are intact.
